problems.title: Weighings
problems.statement: 12 coins, one counterfeit (heavier or lighter, unknown), a balance scale.

parts.prompt: Max coins solvable in 3 weighings for this problem ((3³ − 3)/2)?

problems.solution: 24 ≤ 27, so 3 weighings can suffice (and do, with care); the known maximum is (3ⁿ − 3)/2 = 12.

problems.title: Ropes
problems.statement: Two ropes each burn for exactly 60 minutes, unevenly.

parts.prompt: Light rope A at both ends and B at one end; when A finishes, light B's other end. Total time measured (min)?

hints: Both ends halve the remaining time.
problems.solution: A takes 30; B has 30 left, both ends → 15 more. Total 45.

problems.title: Pirates
problems.statement: 5 pirates (ranked), the top one proposes a split of 100 coins; a majority (ties pass) accepts, otherwise the proposer is thrown overboard. Pirates are rational, greedy, and prefer throwing someone over when indifferent.
problems.solution: Working back: with 2 pirates, the top takes all; with 3, the top gives 1 to the lowest; …; with 5, the top keeps 98 and gives 1 each to pirates 3 and 5 (who'd get 0 otherwise).

problems.title: Hats in a line
problems.statement: n prisoners in a line, each sees those ahead; hats are black or white; each guesses in turn from the back, and everyone hears the guesses.

parts.prompt: Guaranteed correct guesses out of n = 10?

options: the last person announces the parity of black hats they see; everyone deduces their own

problems.solution: Everyone except the first speaker is guaranteed correct.

problems.title: Dominoes
problems.statement: An 8×8 board with two opposite corners removed.
problems.solution: Each domino covers one of each colour; 30 ≠ 32, so no.

problems.title: Bridge crossing
problems.statement: Four people take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes to cross; at most two cross at a time (moving at the slower speed); one torch must accompany each crossing.

problems.title: Two envelopes
problems.statement: One envelope has twice the other. You open one and see $100.

parts.prompt: Is "switch, because E = ½·50 + ½·200 = 125" valid?
options: No: it assumes each case is equally likely for every observed amount, which no proper prior allows

problems.solution: With a proper prior over amounts, the 50/50 assumption fails for some values. Without a prior, there's no reason to switch.
